text:
This is a single-panel line chart showing validation loss over training for three methods.

The horizontal axis is Training step, from 0 to 10,000, with ticks every 2,000. The vertical axis is Cross-entropy loss, shown from about 1.5 to 4.7, with ticks every 0.5. Both axes are linear; the vertical axis does not start at zero.

The three lines are Baseline in blue, + LoRA in orange, and Full fine-tune in green.

All three start at about 4.5 loss. At 10,000 steps, Baseline is about 2.08, + LoRA about 1.85, and Full fine-tune about 1.62. These ending values are also the lowest visible values for each line. Around 2,000 steps, the lines are clustered near 2.7 to 2.8.

Loss falls steeply at first for all three methods, then declines more gradually. The blue Baseline line is generally highest late in training, orange is in the middle, and green is lowest. The lines cross or come close together early on, but separate later, with Full fine-tune ending lowest.

This is a single-panel bar chart comparing ImageNet top-1 accuracy across five models.

The horizontal axis is labeled Model and lists the model names. The vertical axis is labeled Top-1 accuracy, in percent, and runs from 70 to 88 percent in increments of 2; it does not start at zero and is not logarithmic.

The five bars are ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, ConvNeXt-T, Swin-T, and Ours.

Their accuracies are 76.1, 81.8, 82.1, 81.3, and 84.6 percent, respectively. Ours is highest at 84.6 percent, and ResNet-50 is lowest at 76.1 percent.

The four named comparison models cluster between 81.3 and 82.1 percent, while ResNet-50 is noticeably lower. Ours is higher than every comparison model.

This is a grouped bar chart showing scores across three benchmarks for three model sizes.

It has one panel. The horizontal axis is labeled “Benchmark” and lists GLUE, SuperGLUE, and SQuAD F1. The vertical axis is labeled “Score,” with a range from 50 to 100; it starts at 50 rather than zero. No units or logarithmic scale are indicated.

The legend groups the bars by model size: Small, Base, and Large.

For GLUE, the scores are about 78 for Small, 84 for Base, and 89 for Large. For SuperGLUE, they are about 65, 71, and 79. For SQuAD F1, they are about 83, 89, and 91. The lowest score is about 65 for Small on SuperGLUE, and the highest is about 91 for Large on SQuAD F1.

Within every benchmark, scores rise from Small to Base to Large. SQuAD F1 scores are highest overall, while SuperGLUE scores are lowest.

This is a single-panel confusion-matrix heatmap showing the test-set counts for true labels compared with predicted labels.

The horizontal axis is “Predicted label” and the vertical axis is “True label.” Both use the categories cat, dog, bird, and car, with no numerical axis range or units. The color scale runs from 0 to 100, marked in steps of 20; it is not logarithmic.

The four categories, in order on both axes, are cat, dog, bird, and car.

For true cats, the counts predicted as cat, dog, bird, and car are 88, 9, 2, and 1. For true dogs, they are 11, 84, 3, and 2. For true birds, they are 3, 4, 90, and 3. For true cars, they are 0, 1, 2, and 97. The largest value is 97 for cars correctly predicted as cars; the smallest is 0 for cars predicted as cats.

The diagonal values are highest in each row, indicating the most frequent prediction matches the true label. Cars have the highest diagonal count, followed by birds, cats, and dogs. The largest off-diagonal counts are 11 dogs predicted as cats and 9 cats predicted as dogs.

This is a single-panel attention heat map showing how strongly each query token attends to each key token.

The horizontal axis is Key token and the vertical axis is Query token. Both axes show the seven tokens, in order: “The,” “cat,” “sat,” “on,” “the,” “mat,” and a period. The color scale runs from 0 to 1; the axes are categorical, not numeric.

The panel is titled “Layer 6, head 3 attention.” There is no separate legend; the color bar indicates attention strength, from dark purple near zero to yellow at 1.

The strongest cell is “The” attending to “The,” at 1.0. Other strong diagonal values are about 0.9 for “cat” to “cat,” 0.8 for “sat” to “sat,” 0.85 for “on” to “on,” and 0.75 for “the” to “the.” The “mat” query attends most to “cat,” at about 0.45, and to “mat,” at about 0.35. The period query attends most to itself, at about 0.6. Most remaining cells are below about 0.15.

Overall, attention is concentrated along the diagonal for the first five tokens. The main off-diagonal exception is “mat” attending to “cat.”

This is a single scatter plot showing MMLU scores against parameter count for three model families.

The horizontal axis is Parameters (B), ranging from about 3 to 72 billion, with labeled ticks from 10 to 70; it is linear and does not start at zero. The vertical axis is MMLU (percent), ranging from about 55 to 88 percent, with labeled ticks from 55 to 85; it is linear and also does not start at zero.

The legend groups the points into Dense, shown as blue circles; MoE, shown as orange crosses; and Distilled, shown as green squares.

Dense scores range from about 57 percent at 6 billion parameters to about 87 percent at 65 billion. MoE ranges from about 56 percent at 6 billion to about 87 percent at 66 billion. Distilled ranges from about 61 percent at 11 billion to about 82 percent at 68 billion. There are no connecting lines.

Scores generally rise as parameter count increases. MoE is often highest in the middle parameter range, while Dense and MoE reach similar top scores at the largest counts. Distilled scores are generally lower, particularly at high parameter counts.

This is a box-and-whisker chart comparing inference latency across four hardware types.

The horizontal axis is Hardware, with categories rather than a numeric scale. The vertical axis is Latency in milliseconds; it starts at zero, is not logarithmic, and has labeled ticks every 25 milliseconds from zero to 175, with the plot extending to about 200.

The groups are CPU, GPU, TPU, and Edge NPU.

For CPU, the median is about 116 milliseconds, the box spans about 106 to 141, and the whiskers run from about 68 to 190. GPU has a median near 16, a box from about 14 to 20, whiskers from about 10 to 27, and one outlier near 29. TPU has a median near 11, a box from about 9 to 14, whiskers from about 6 to 20, and outliers around 22 to 24. Edge NPU has a median near 44, a box from about 37 to 48, whiskers from about 23 to 62, and several high outliers, from about 64 up to 87.

CPU has the highest typical latency and widest spread. TPU has the lowest median, followed by GPU. Edge NPU is between those groups, with several high outliers.

This is a set of three split violin plots comparing score distributions with and without chain-of-thought prompting across three tasks.

The horizontal axis is Task, with Math, Code, and Writing; it has no numeric scale. The vertical axis is Score, with labeled ticks from 20 to 100 in steps of 20. It is a linear scale and does not start at zero; the plotted range extends from about 18 to 110.

The legend names the blue half Without CoT and the orange half With CoT. Each violin shows a distribution, with dashed lines marking the lower quartile, median, and upper quartile.

For Math, the medians are about 55 without CoT and 74 with CoT; the quartile ranges are about 48 to 62 and 67 to 79. For Code, the medians are about 54 and 64, with quartile ranges of about 49 to 62 and 58 to 70. For Writing, the medians are about 54 and 56, with ranges of about 48 to 61 and 47 to 64.

With CoT scores are higher in Math and Code, especially in Math. Writing scores are similar between conditions, with broadly overlapping distributions.

This is an overlaid histogram with smooth density curves, showing the distributions of logit margins for two splits.

The horizontal axis is labeled “Logit margin,” runs from about minus 3.5 to 5, and is linear. The vertical axis is labeled “Count,” runs from 0 to about 185, and is also linear.

The two groups are In-distribution, shown in blue, and Out-of-distribution, shown in orange.

The tallest blue bar is about 175, near a logit margin of minus 0.3; its smooth curve peaks near 160. The tallest orange bar is about 135, near 3; its curve peaks at about the same level. Blue counts extend roughly from minus 3 to 2.5, while orange counts extend roughly from 1.5 to 4.5.

The blue distribution is concentrated around values near zero, mostly below 1. The orange distribution is concentrated around 3, with higher margins overall. They overlap mainly between about 1.5 and 2.5, where both counts are relatively low.

This is a single-panel scatter plot with a fitted line, showing a strong positive relationship between GPU hours and throughput.

The horizontal axis is GPU hours, in thousands, ranging from 0 to 10. The vertical axis is tokens per second, in thousands; it does not start at zero and spans roughly 1 to 27.

The plot shows blue data points and a blue upward-sloping fitted line with a pale shaded band around it.

The points range from about 0.05 thousand GPU hours and 6 thousand tokens per second to about 9.9 thousand GPU hours and 23 thousand tokens per second. The lowest throughput is about 2.5 thousand tokens per second, near 0.65 thousand GPU hours. The highest is about 26 thousand, near 8.6 thousand GPU hours. The fitted line rises from about 5.5 thousand tokens per second at zero GPU hours to about 24.5 thousand at roughly 9.8 thousand GPU hours. The title reports a correlation of 0.94.

Overall, throughput generally increases as GPU hours increase. The points cluster around the fitted line, though there is noticeable variation, including a low point near 6.2 thousand GPU hours and 12.7 thousand tokens per second.

This is a line chart showing how test error changes as dataset size increases for three optimizers.

There is one panel. The horizontal axis is Dataset size, in tokens, and runs from 1 million to 10 billion on a logarithmic scale. The vertical axis is Error, ranging from about 0.75 to 3.15; it does not start at zero.

The three series are SGD, Adam, and Muon.

At 1 million tokens, all three are near 3.0 error. At 10 billion tokens, SGD is about 1.34, Adam about 1.15, and Muon about 0.91. At the intermediate dataset sizes, the approximate errors for SGD are 2.70, 2.42, 2.26, 1.99, 1.79, 1.63, and 1.50. For Adam they are 2.64, 2.30, 2.07, 1.88, 1.66, 1.45, and 1.29. For Muon they are 2.60, 2.27, 1.95, 1.70, 1.45, 1.26, and 1.06.

Error decreases for all three as dataset size grows. The lines are close at the smallest size, then Muon is generally lowest, Adam is in the middle, and SGD is highest.

This is a two-panel line chart showing accuracy across training epochs and final validation accuracy at different learning rates.

In panel A, the horizontal axis is Epoch, from 0 to 30, and the vertical axis is Accuracy, displayed from about 0.23 to 1.03, so it does not start at zero. A dashed vertical line marks epoch 12. In panel B, the horizontal axis is Learning rate on a logarithmic scale, with values from 10 to the minus 4 through 10 to the minus 2. The vertical axis is Final validation accuracy, displayed from about 0.61 to 0.90, so it also does not start at zero.

Panel A has two series: Train and Validation. Panel B shows validation accuracy at five learning rates.

The training curve starts near 0.26 and ends near 1.00. The validation curve starts near 0.26, is about 0.91 at epoch 12, peaks near 0.95 around epoch 17, and ends near 0.87. In panel B, the values are about 0.81 at 10 to the minus 4, 0.86 at 3 times 10 to the minus 4, 0.89 at 10 to the minus 3, 0.84 at 3 times 10 to the minus 3, and 0.62 at 10 to the minus 2.

Both curves in panel A rise quickly at first; training continues upward while validation declines after its peak. In panel B, accuracy peaks at the middle learning rate and drops sharply at the highest one.

This is a three-panel line chart showing accuracy over training epochs for three datasets, with and without RandAugment.

Each panel has Epoch on the horizontal axis, from 0 to 100, and Accuracy on the vertical axis, with labeled ticks from 0.0 to 0.8; the plotted range extends to about 1.0. Neither axis is logarithmic. The panels, from left to right, are CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet.

The two series in every panel are None, shown in blue, and RandAugment, shown in orange.

All lines start at zero. At epoch 100, CIFAR-10 is about 0.91 for None and 0.94 for RandAugment. CIFAR-100 is about 0.69 and 0.75, respectively. Tiny-ImageNet is about 0.55 and 0.60. The highest endpoint is RandAugment on CIFAR-10; the lowest is None on Tiny-ImageNet.

Accuracy rises quickly in the early epochs, then gains slow. RandAugment is consistently slightly higher than None after the start, and both methods rank the datasets in the same order: CIFAR-10 highest, CIFAR-100 next, and Tiny-ImageNet lowest.

This is an error-bar chart showing mean BLEU scores for four model variants, with standard deviations over five seeds.

The horizontal axis is labeled Variant and has four categories. The vertical axis is labeled BLEU; it has no units, uses a linear scale, and does not start at zero. The visible scale runs from about 55 to 74, with labeled ticks from 57.5 to 72.5 in steps of 2.5.

The categories are Full model, minus attention, minus residual, and minus norm. There is no separate legend.

The mean scores are about 71.5 for Full model, 65.3 for minus attention, 56.5 for minus residual, and 66.6 for minus norm. The error bars span about 70.3 to 72.8, 64.2 to 66.4, 56.2 to 56.9, and 65.0 to 68.2, respectively.

The Full model has the highest mean, and minus residual has the lowest by a wide margin. Minus norm scores about 1.3 points higher than minus attention. The residual variant also has the smallest error bar, while minus norm has the largest.

This is a three-by-three scatterplot matrix showing petal and sepal measurements for three species groups, with each variable’s distribution shown along the diagonal.

The horizontal axes, from left to right, are petal length, petal width, and sepal length; the vertical axes, from top to bottom, are the same three measurements. No measurement units are given. The scales are linear. Petal length runs from near zero to about seven, petal width from near zero to about two point four, and sepal length from about four to eight. So the sepal-length axes do not start at zero. The diagonal panels show distributions rather than scatter points.

The legend names the blue setosa-like group, the orange versicolor-like group, and the green virginica-like group.

Setosa-like measurements cluster around petal lengths of one to two, petal widths of about zero point one to zero point five, and sepal lengths of about four point three to five point eight. Versicolor-like points cluster around petal lengths of four to five, widths of about one to one point eight, and sepal lengths of about five to seven point one. Virginica-like points cluster around petal lengths of five to seven, widths of about one point four to two point three, and sepal lengths of about six to seven point three.

Overall, setosa-like points are clearly separated at smaller petal measurements. Versicolor-like and virginica-like points have larger measurements and overlap more, though virginica-like points generally have larger petals and sepals. The orange sepal-length maximum near seven point one is a visible high point.

This is a clustered heat map showing normalized scores for five methods across six task categories.

There is one panel. The horizontal axis lists task categories and the vertical axis lists methods; both are categorical, with no units or numeric range. The color scale runs from about zero at dark blue to one at dark red, with a midpoint at 0.5; it is not logarithmic. Dendrograms show clustering along the top and left sides.

The methods are M3, M4, M2, M1, and M5. The task categories are Trans., Code, Math, Summ., QA, and NLI.

Approximate scores by method, in that task order, are: M3, 0.75, 1.0, 0.85, 0.4, 0.05, and 0.05; M4, 0.55, 0.9, 0.9, 0.5, 0.35, and 0.15; M2, 0.15, 0.25, 0.25, 0.5, 0.8, and 0.4; M1, 0.35, 0.1, 0.15, 0.9, 0.6, and 0.7; M5, 0.25, 0.05, 0.2, 0.85, 0.7, and 0.8.

M3 has the highest score, about 1.0 on Code, while M5 is lowest there at about 0.05. M3 and M4 are strongest on Code and Math, while M1 and M5 are stronger on Summ., QA, and NLI. Trans. and Math scores are relatively low for M2, M1, and M5.

This is a single-panel cumulative distribution chart showing the proportion of responses at or below different generated lengths for two decoding methods.

The horizontal axis is labeled “Tokens generated” and runs from zero to about 1,650 tokens, with ticks every 200; it is linear. The vertical axis is labeled “Proportion” and runs from zero to 1.0 in steps of 0.2; it is also linear and starts at zero.

The legend names two lines: Greedy in blue and Speculative in orange.

Speculative reaches a proportion of about 0.5 at 100 tokens, 0.8 at 180, and 0.9 at 230, then approaches 1.0 by about 400 tokens. Greedy reaches about 0.2 at 130 tokens, 0.4 at 200, 0.6 at 300, 0.8 at 440, and 0.9 at 550. It approaches 1.0 around 1,000 tokens.

Both lines start near zero. The orange Speculative line rises faster and stays to the left of the blue Greedy line, indicating shorter response lengths overall. Greedy has a longer tail, extending to roughly 1,000 tokens, while Speculative levels off by roughly 400 tokens.

This is a horizontal bar chart showing the number of papers in the survey for six venues.

The horizontal axis is labeled “count,” runs from zero to about 430, and has ticks every 50; it is linear and starts at zero. The vertical axis is labeled “Venue” and lists the categories.

There is no separate legend; the bars represent NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL, CVPR, and EMNLP, from top to bottom.

The approximate counts are: NeurIPS 411, ICML 304, ICLR 376, ACL 157, CVPR 289, and EMNLP 132.

NeurIPS has the most papers, followed by ICLR, ICML, CVPR, ACL, and EMNLP. The values vary considerably, with a large gap between the four higher-count venues and ACL and EMNLP.
